# Dropoff

> Dropoff is a free, secure, zero-backend file sharing tool that sends files directly between browsers over an encrypted peer-to-peer WebRTC connection. Everything runs client-side, so files are never uploaded to or stored on a server.

Full details about the service, how it works, its limits, and its privacy model.

## Overview

Dropoff is a free, browser-based file sharing tool. A sender opens Dropoff, picks one or more files, and the site generates a one-time `dropoff.lol/receive/<id>` link. Anyone who opens that link receives the files directly from the sender's browser. The transfer is peer to peer and never touches a Dropoff server.

Dropoff is a zero-backend, client-side web utility built on WebRTC. It requires a modern browser and works on Windows, macOS, Linux, iOS, and Android.

## Why it exists

Most file sharing services upload your files to a cloud server first. That means files sit on someone else's infrastructure, may be scanned or retained, and are often tied to accounts. Dropoff takes a different approach: nothing is uploaded and nothing is stored, because the transferring browsers act as the servers. Files go directly from one device to another.

## How it works

1. A sender opens https://www.dropoff.lol and picks one or more files.
2. Dropoff connects the sender to a lightweight signaling server only to bootstrap a peer-to-peer WebRTC connection, then generates a link formatted `dropoff.lol/receive/<id>`.
3. The sender shares that link with the receiver by any means.
4. The receiver opens the link and the files stream directly, device to device.
5. When the transfer finishes, the link is no longer needed. Nothing was uploaded or stored by Dropoff.

## Privacy and security

- Transfers use WebRTC, which encrypts peer-to-peer traffic in transit.
- Share links are random one-time URLs, so a transfer cannot be guessed or enumerated.
- There are no accounts, no file retention, and no cloud storage.
- Dropoff does not scan, log, or read the contents of transferred files.

## Limits and requirements

- File size is constrained by the browser, not by Dropoff (there is no upload, so there is no server cap). Practical limits are roughly 1–2 GB on desktop Chrome, about 1 GB on Firefox, and a few hundred MB on iPhone/iOS Safari.
- The sender's tab must stay open for the duration of the transfer, because the sender's browser is the source of the files.
- Both sides need an internet connection; the transfer is end to end between the browsers.
